claim: MicroRNA-146a (miR-146a) is a critical negative regulator of inflammation.
source: MicroRNA-146a (miR-146a) is a critical negative regulator of inflammation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about miR-146a's function.

claim: Deletion of miR-146a produces effects that appear as dysregulated inflammatory hematopoiesis.
source: Deletion of miR-146a produces effects that appear as dysregulated inflammatory hematopoiesis, leading to a decline in the number and quality of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), excessive myeloproliferation, and, ultimately, to HSC exhaustion and hematopoietic neoplasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract describing the phenotype of miR-146a knockout mice.

claim: Deletion of miR-146a leads to a decline in the number and quality of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
source: Deletion of miR-146a produces effects that appear as dysregulated inflammatory hematopoiesis, leading to a decline in the number and quality of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), excessive myeloproliferation, and, ultimately, to HSC exhaustion and hematopoietic neoplasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of miR-146a leads to excessive myeloproliferation.
source: Deletion of miR-146a produces effects that appear as dysregulated inflammatory hematopoiesis, leading to a decline in the number and quality of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), excessive myeloproliferation, and, ultimately, to HSC exhaustion and hematopoietic neoplasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of miR-146a ultimately leads to HSC exhaustion and hematopoietic neoplasms.
source: Deletion of miR-146a produces effects that appear as dysregulated inflammatory hematopoiesis, leading to a decline in the number and quality of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), excessive myeloproliferation, and, ultimately, to HSC exhaustion and hematopoietic neoplasms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The defects in miR-146a-deficient mice are attributable to both an intrinsic problem in the miR-146a–deficient HSCs and extrinsic effects of lymphocytes and nonhematopoietic cells.
source: At the cellular level, the defects are attributable to both an intrinsic problem in the miR-146a–deficient HSCs and extrinsic effects of lymphocytes and nonhematopoietic cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transplantation experiments in the manuscript.

claim: The molecular mechanism involves a molecular axis consisting of miR-146a, signaling protein TRAF6, transcriptional factor NF-κB, and cytokine IL-6.
source: At the molecular level, this involves a molecular axis consisting of miR-146a, signaling protein TRAF6, transcriptional factor NF-κB, and cytokine IL-6.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic and molecular data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MiR-146a is a critical regulator of HSC homeostasis during chronic inflammation in mice.
source: This study has identified miR-146a to be a critical regulator of HSC homeostasis during chronic inflammation in mice and provided a molecular connection between chronic inflammation and the development of bone marrow failure and myeloproliferative neoplasms.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: This study provides a molecular connection between chronic inflammation and the development of bone marrow failure and myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source: This study has identified miR-146a to be a critical regulator of HSC homeostasis during chronic inflammation in mice and provided a molecular connection between chronic inflammation and the development of bone marrow failure and myeloproliferative neoplasms.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: HSCs have the ability to self-renew and replenish the entire hematopoietic repertoire during the lifetime of an organism.
source: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) have the ability to self-renew and replenish the entire hematopoietic repertoire during the lifetime of an organism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSCs cited from the literature (Seita and Weissman, 2010).

claim: Under stressed conditions such as inflammation and infection, the balance is shifted in favor of HSPC proliferation and differentiation to produce more mature immune cells.
source: Under stressed conditions, such as inflammation and infection, the balance is shifted in favor of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) proliferation and differentiation to produce more mature immune cells (King and Goodell, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (King and Goodell, 2011).

claim: HSCs express TLRs and may sense and respond to infection and inflammatory signals directly.
source: Following the discovery that HSCs express TLRs and may sense and respond to infection and inflammatory signals directly (Nagai et al., 2006), there has been an increasing appreciation of the role of proinflammatory cytokines and infection in the modulation of HSC activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Nagai et al., 2006).

claim: TLR activation or interferon stimulation leads to proliferation, skewed myeloid differentiation and impaired engraftment, and self-renewal of HSCs.
source: Numerous recent studies have shown that TLR activation or interferon stimulation leads to proliferation, skewed myeloid differentiation and impaired engraftment, and self-renewal of HSCs (Essers et al., 2009; Baldridge et al., 2010; Esplin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple literature sources (Essers et al., 2009; Baldridge et al., 2010; Esplin et al., 2011).

claim: NF-κB has been shown to be active in a wide variety of innate and adaptive immune cells as well as nonhematopoietic cells.
source: Since its discovery over 25 years ago, NF-κB has been shown to be active in a wide variety of innate and adaptive immune cells as well as nonhematopoietic cells and to function as an essential player in orchestrating inflammation and immune cell functions (Baltimore, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Baltimore, 2011).

claim: NF-κB functions as an essential player in orchestrating inflammation and immune cell functions.
source: Since its discovery over 25 years ago, NF-κB has been shown to be active in a wide variety of innate and adaptive immune cells as well as nonhematopoietic cells and to function as an essential player in orchestrating inflammation and immune cell functions (Baltimore, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Baltimore, 2011).

claim: Under stress-free conditions, NF-κB is not essential for HSC function.
source: Under stress-free conditions, NF-κB is not essential for HSC function, because mice genetically deleted for NF-κB subunits, such as Nfkb1 (also known as p50) and Rel (also known as c-Rel), have no apparent developmental abnormality in the hematopoietic system.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Gerondakis et al., 2012).

claim: Mice genetically deleted for NF-κB subunits, such as Nfkb1 (also known as p50) and Rel (also known as c-Rel), have no apparent developmental abnormality in the hematopoietic system.
source: Under stress-free conditions, NF-κB is not essential for HSC function, because mice genetically deleted for NF-κB subunits, such as Nfkb1 (also known as p50) and Rel (also known as c-Rel), have no apparent developmental abnormality in the hematopoietic system.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Gerondakis et al., 2012).

claim: Mice engrafted with p50 or c-Rel knockout HSCs or RelA knockout fetal HSCs develop relatively normal immune system under stress-free conditions.
source: Mice engrafted with p50 or c-Rel knockout HSCs or RelA knockout fetal HSCs also develop relatively normal immune system under stress-free conditions (Gerondakis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Gerondakis et al., 2012).

claim: Mice with activated NF-κB signaling display severe inflammation, early lethality, and complex phenotypes.
source: However, mice with activated NF-κB signaling, as a consequence of deleting IκBα, A20, or the inhibitory domain of p50 or p52 subunits of NF-κB, display severe inflammation, early lethality, and complex phenotypes, making studies of HSCs difficult to perform and interpret (Lee et al., 2000; Gerondakis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Lee et al., 2000; Gerondakis et al., 2006).

claim: MiR-146a has been shown to be a particularly important negative regulator of NF-κB by targeting two upstream signal transducers, TRAF6 and IRAK1.
source: Among them, miR-146a has been shown to be a particularly important negative regulator of NF-κB by targeting two upstream signal transducers, TRAF6 and IRAK1.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Boldin and Baltimore, 2012).

claim: Mice with targeted miR-146a deletion represent one of the first genetic mouse models with NF-κB-driven chronic and low-grade inflammation that develops spontaneously with aging.
source: Mice with targeted miR-146a deletion represent one of the first genetic mouse models with NF-κB-driven chronic and low-grade inflammation that develops spontaneously with aging and can be accelerated by repeated stimulation, allowing investigation of the long-term effects of chronic inflammation and NF-κB activation on HSCs and oncogenic processes (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: Chronic inflammation in miR-146a-deficient mice can be accelerated by repeated stimulation.
source: Mice with targeted miR-146a deletion represent one of the first genetic mouse models with NF-κB-driven chronic and low-grade inflammation that develops spontaneously with aging and can be accelerated by repeated stimulation, allowing investigation of the long-term effects of chronic inflammation and NF-κB activation on HSCs and oncogenic processes (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: MiR-146a and miR-146b are expressed at variable levels throughout hematopoietic development.
source: We found that miR-146a and miR-146b were expressed at variable levels throughout hematopoietic development.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The expression of miR-146a increased by twofold as long-term HSCs differentiated into a mixed pool of short-term HSCs and multipotent progenitor cells (LSK cells).
source: The expression of miR-146a increased by twofold as long-term HSCs (defined as Lineage−Sca1+cKit+ CD150+CD48−) differentiated into a mixed pool of short-term HSCs and multipotent progenitor cells (MPPs) (defined by Lineage−Sca1+cKit+, referred to as LSK cells).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The lowest expression of miR-146a was detected in myeloid progenitor cells (defined by Lineage−Sca1−cKit+, referred to as L−S−K+ cells).
source: The lowest expression of miR-146a was detected in myeloid progenitor cells (defined by Lineage−Sca1−cKit+, referred to as L−S−K+ cells) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MiR-146b expression was more uniform throughout hematopoietic development compared to miR-146a.
source: In comparison, miR-146b expression was more uniform throughout hematopoietic development (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MiR-146a and miR-146b could be functional in cells as primitive as the long-term HSCs and throughout hematopoietic development.
source: This expression pattern suggests that miR-146a and miR-146b could be functional in cells as primitive as the long-term HSCs and throughout hematopoietic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Deleting miR-146a has no detectable effect on hematopoiesis early on in life in a standard pathogen-free environment.
source: These data indicate that deleting miR-146a has no detectable effect on hematopoiesis early on in life in a standard pathogen-free environment.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from 6-week-old mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: MiR-146a KO mice develop spontaneous inflammation as they age.
source: We have previously shown that miR-146a KO mice develop spontaneous inflammation as they age (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: By 4 months, miR-146a KO mice developed a mildly hypercellular bone marrow indicated by an increase in total bone marrow CD45+ cells, LSK cells, and long-term HSCs.
source: By 4 months, miR-146a KO mice developed a mildly hypercellular bone marrow indicated by an increase in total bone marrow CD45+ cells, LSK cells, and long-term HSCs, with unaltered percentages of CD19+, CD11b+ and CD3ε+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: By 8 months of age, miR-146a KO mice showed a significant decrease in the number of total bone marrow cells and phenotypically defined HSPCs, including LSK cells and CD150+CD48− or EPCR+ long-term HSCs.
source: By 8 months of age, miR-146a KO mice showed a significant decrease in the number of total bone marrow cells and phenotypically defined HSPCs, including LSK cells and CD150+CD48− or EPCR+ long-term HSCs (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: By 12 months of age, the majority of miR-146a KO mice showed only a residual number of CD45+ bone marrow cells and nearly complete exhaustion of HSCs.
source: The depletion became progressively more severe by 12 months of age when the majority of miR-146a KO mice showed only a residual number of CD45+ bone marrow cells and nearly complete exhaustion of HSCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 8-month-old miR-146a KO mice showed an increased percent of LSK cells within the total bone marrow but a significantly decreased fraction of long-term HSCs among the LSK cells.
source: Dysregulated hematopoiesis was observed in 8-month-old KO mice, as shown by an increased percent of LSK cells within the total bone marrow but a significantly decreased fraction of long-term HSCs among the LSK cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MiR-146a KO mice showed a significant increase in the number of LSK cells and long-term HSCs in their spleens.
source: In addition, miR-146a KO mice also showed a significant increase in the number of LSK cells and long-term HSCs in their spleens, which may be due to HSPC mobilization from bone marrow to spleen and/or de novo splenic HSPC proliferation in response to bone marrow failure (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: When total HSCs from the marrow and spleen of the same mice were summed, a reduction in HSC number was still apparent.
source: Furthermore, when total HSCs from the marrow and spleen of the same mice were summed, a reduction in HSC number was still apparent (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Chronic inflammatory stimulation with bacterial components in young miR-146a KO mice was sufficient to accelerate the development of the same hematopoietic defects seen during aging of these mice.
source: Importantly, we found that chronic inflammatory stimulation with bacterial components in young miR-146a KO mice was sufficient to accelerate the development of the same hematopoietic defects seen during aging of these mice.
evidence: This is supported by LPS stimulation experiments shown in Figure 1H–J.

claim: MiR-146a is needed to maintain HSC homeostasis in response to chronic inflammation.
source: Thus, miR-146a is needed to maintain HSC homeostasis in response to chronic inflammation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LPS stimulation experiments shown in Figure 1H–J.

claim: 6 months after transplant, CD45.2+ and CD45.1+ cells in both the CD45.2 WT/CD45.1 WT and CD45.2 KO/CD45.1 WT mice contributed identical proportions of cells in nearly all mature hematopoietic lineages and HSPCs.
source: 6 months after transplant, CD45.2+ and CD45.1+ cells in both the CD45.2 WT/CD45.1 WT and CD45.2 KO/CD45.1 WT mice contributed identical proportions of cells in nearly all mature hematopoietic lineages and HSPCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by competitive repopulation assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When competitive repopulation assay was extended past 10 months, a decreased contribution of miR-146a KO cells to long-term HSCs and LSK cells was observed, but no reduction in CD45+ cells.
source: However, when we extended the experiment past 10 months, we began to observe a decreased contribution of miR-146a KO cells to long-term HSCs and LSK cells, but no reduction in CD45+ cells, in the bone marrow of CD45.2 KO/CD45.1 WT mice (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by competitive repopulation assay data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: MiR-146a-deficient long-term HSCs from young mice have an intrinsic defect and are more susceptible to depletion compared to WT HSCs in the same environment.
source: These data indicate that miR-146a-deficient long-term HSCs from young mice have an intrinsic defect and are more susceptible to depletion compared to WT HSCs in the same environment; however, the intrinsic defect of miR-146a KO HSCs from young mice is rather modest and takes 10 months to become apparent in this transplant setting.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on competitive repopulation assay data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: The intrinsic defect of miR-146a KO HSCs from young mice is rather modest and takes 10 months to become apparent in the transplant setting.
source: These data indicate that miR-146a-deficient long-term HSCs from young mice have an intrinsic defect and are more susceptible to depletion compared to WT HSCs in the same environment; however, the intrinsic defect of miR-146a KO HSCs from young mice is rather modest and takes 10 months to become apparent in this transplant setting.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on competitive repopulation assay data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: When competitive repopulation experiment was carried out with 4-month-old WT and miR-146a KO bone marrow cells, miR-146a KO cells were outcompeted by their WT counterparts as early as the first month after the transplant.
source: Surprisingly, miR-146a KO cells were outcompeted by their WT counterparts as early as the first month after the transplant, and there was a steady decline in their percentage over a period of 6 months (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is supported by competitive repopulation assay data shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: The functional quality of HSCs became more and more compromised as miR-146a KO mice aged.
source: Similar to the progressive decline of HSC number, the functional quality of HSCs became more and more compromised as miR-146a KO mice aged.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on competitive repopulation assays with mice of different ages shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mice of the WT to WT and WT to KO groups had identical levels of HSPCs in their bone marrows and spleens.
source: Interestingly, mice of the WT to WT and WT to KO groups had identical levels of HSPCs in their bone marrows and spleens, suggesting that the miR-146a-deficient environment is not sufficient to induce significant HSC abnormalities in WT cells during this time (Figure 3A–G).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3A–G.

claim: The miR-146a-deficient environment is not sufficient to induce significant HSC abnormalities in WT cells during 5 months after transplant.
source: Interestingly, mice of the WT to WT and WT to KO groups had identical levels of HSPCs in their bone marrows and spleens, suggesting that the miR-146a-deficient environment is not sufficient to induce significant HSC abnormalities in WT cells during this time (Figure 3A–G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3A–G.

claim: Mice in the KO to WT and KO to KO groups both showed twofold to threefold reductions in bone marrow HSCs and myeloid progenitor cells, but not in LSK cells.
source: In comparison, mice in the KO to WT and KO to KO groups both showed twofold to threefold reductions in bone marrow HSCs and myeloid progenitor cells, but not in LSK cells (Figure 3A–C), and about a 10-fold increase in spleen HSPCs (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3A–G.

claim: Mice in the KO to WT and KO to KO groups showed about a 10-fold increase in spleen HSPCs.
source: In comparison, mice in the KO to WT and KO to KO groups both showed twofold to threefold reductions in bone marrow HSCs and myeloid progenitor cells, but not in LSK cells (Figure 3A–C), and about a 10-fold increase in spleen HSPCs (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: It is the miR-146a deficiency in hematopoietic cells that plays the dominant role in determining the phenotype of the miR-146a knockout mouse.
source: These data indicate that it is the miR-146a deficiency in hematopoietic cells that plays the dominant role in determining the phenotype of the miR-146a knockout mouse, because transferring miR-146a-deficient bone marrow cells into WT environment, but not the reciprocal transfer, is sufficient to yield a majority of the phenotypes seen in mice with miR-146a deleted in both hematopoietic and nonhematopoietic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The miR-146a-deficient environment has a contributory role to the overall enhanced myelopoiesis.
source: However, the miR-146a-deficient environment has a contributory role to the overall enhanced myelopoiesis because WT bone marrow cells in the KO environment gave rise to a mild but statistically significant increase in the number of CD45+ and CD11b+ marrow cells and the percentage of CD11b+ and Gr1+ cells in their spleens, compared to the WT to WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L,O,P).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L,O,P.

claim: WT bone marrow cells that were transiently transplanted into miR-146a KO environment for 2 months showed a modest advantage in generating myeloid and lymphoid lineages in their spleens, peripheral blood and to a lesser extent bone marrows.
source: More indicative is that when WT bone marrow cells that were transiently transplanted into miR-146a KO environment for 2 months were competed against WT control bone marrow cells (Figure 3K), they showed a modest advantage in generating myeloid and lymphoid lineages in their spleens, peripheral blood and to a lesser extent bone marrows, whereas bone marrow HSPCs remained unaffected (Figure 3L–O).
evidence: This is supported by serial bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3K–O.

claim: Hematopoietic-intrinsic deficiency of miR-146a plays the dominant role in driving the HSC defects and pathological myeloproliferation.
source: Overall, we have shown that hematopoietic-intrinsic deficiency of miR-146a plays the dominant role in driving the HSC defects and pathological myeloproliferation while the miR-146a deficient environment also contributes to the overall phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The miR-146a deficient environment also contributes to the overall phenotype.
source: Overall, we have shown that hematopoietic-intrinsic deficiency of miR-146a plays the dominant role in driving the HSC defects and pathological myeloproliferation while the miR-146a deficient environment also contributes to the overall phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on reciprocal bone marrow transplant data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MiR-146a–deficient lymphocytes display a hyperactivated phenotype with dysregulated cytokine production.
source: Because miR-146a–deficient lymphocytes display a hyperactivated phenotype with dysregulated cytokine production (Yang et al., 2012), we first determined whether dysregulation of miR-146a-deficient lymphocytes might contribute to HSC depletion in miR-146a KO mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work (Yang et al., 2012).

claim: Long-term HSCs and LSK cells in the miR KO marrow were reduced to only 3% and 15% of the respective WT levels in 10-month-old mice.
source: Specifically, long-term HSCs and LSK cells in the miR KO marrow were reduced to only 3% and 15% of the respective WT levels.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from 10-month-old mice shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Depletion of HSPCs in miR/Rag1 DKO bone marrow was partially rescued compared to miR KO mice.
source: In comparison, depletion of HSPCs in miR/Rag1 DKO bone marrow was partially rescued. Long-term HSCs and LSK cells in miR/Rag1 DKO bone marrow rose to 30% and 50% of the Rag1 KO levels, respectively, and the numbers of myeloid progenitor cells and total white blood cells were normal (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: MiR-146a-deficient lymphocytes contribute substantially to the overall HSPC exhaustion.
source: These data indicate that miR-146a-deficient lymphocytes contribute substantially to the overall HSPC exhaustion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the partial rescue of HSPC depletion in miR/Rag1 DKO mice shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: MiR-146a-deficient lymphocytes were shown to be a major driver of the development of bone marrow failure and myeloproliferative disease.
source: In addition, miR-146a-deficient lymphocytes were shown to be a major driver of the development of bone marrow failure and myeloproliferative disease, because miR/Rag1 DKO mice showed normal bone marrow cellularity and an attenuated splenomegaly and myeloproliferative phenotype (Figure 4E–L).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the attenuated phenotype in miR/Rag1 DKO mice shown in Figure 4E–L.

claim: MiR-146a deficiency in myeloid lineages has an intrinsic effect on the development of myeloproliferation.
source: However, the rescue was not complete because miR/Rag1 DKO mice still had mildly enlarged spleens and a twofold to threefold increase in the number of total white blood cells and myeloid cells compared to Rag1 KO mice, indicating that miR-146a deficiency in myeloid lineages has an intrinsic effect on the development of myeloproliferation (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the incomplete rescue in miR/Rag1 DKO mice shown in Figure 4M.

claim: About 6–7% of WT LSK cells and HSCs had basally activated NF-κB activity in 2-month-old WT NF-κB-GFP reporter mice.
source: We found that about 6–7% of WT LSK cells and HSCs had basally activated NF-κB activity, as measured by GFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from NF-κB-GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 6 hr after LPS challenge in vivo, the percentage of LSK cells and HSCs with activated NF-κB increased to more than 25%.
source: 6 hr after LPS challenge in vivo, the percentage of LSK cells and HSCs with activated NF-κB increased to more than 25% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from NF-κB-GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 8-month-old WT-GFP mice showed an increased percentage of LSK cells and HSCs with basal NF-κB activation, compared to 2-month-old mice.
source: Interestingly, 8-month-old WT-GFP mice also showed an increased percentage of LSK cells and HSCs with basal NF-κB activation, compared to 2-month-old mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from NF-κB-GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both LSK cells and HSCs have functional NF-κB–mediated transcription that can be augmented by LPS stimulation and aging.
source: These data suggest that both LSK cells and HSCs have functional NF-κB–mediated transcription that can be augmented by LPS stimulation and aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NF-κB-GFP reporter data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After repeated LPS stimulation, miRKO-GFP mice showed increased percentages of GFP+ cells in various HSPCs compared to WT-GFP and miRHET-GFP mice.
source: After repeated LPS stimulation, miRKO-GFP mice, in comparison to WT-GFP and miRHET-GFP mice, showed increased percentages of GFP+ cells in various HSPCs (Figure 5A–C) and mature cells in their bone marrows, spleens and peripheral blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C), demonstrating that chronic inflammatory stimulation with bacterial components leads to hyperactivated NF-κB activity in young miR-146a-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from NF-κB-GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Chronic inflammatory stimulation with bacterial components leads to hyperactivated NF-κB activity in young miR-146a-deficient mice.
source: After repeated LPS stimulation, miRKO-GFP mice, in comparison to WT-GFP and miRHET-GFP mice, showed increased percentages of GFP+ cells in various HSPCs (Figure 5A–C) and mature cells in their bone marrows, spleens and peripheral blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C), demonstrating that chronic inflammatory stimulation with bacterial components leads to hyperactivated NF-κB activity in young miR-146a-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NF-κB-GFP reporter data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: By 8–9 months of age, miR/p50 DKO mice still exhibited levels of white blood cells and long-term HSCs comparable to that of WT mice, indicating a rescue of the HSC defects.
source: By 8–9 months of age, miR/p50 DKO mice still exhibited levels of white blood cells and long-term HSCs comparable to that of WT mice, indicating a rescue of the HSC defects (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: P50 deletion rescues the myeloproliferative disease in 6-month-old miR-146a KO mice.
source: We have previously shown that p50 deletion rescues the myeloproliferative disease in 6-month-old miR-146a KO mice (Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work (Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: MiR/p50 DKO mice showed reduced spleen weight and prolonged survival compared to miR KO mice.
source: Interestingly, miR/p50 DKO mice still showed reduced spleen weight and prolonged survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The incidence of tumors was significantly reduced in miR/p50 DKO mice, compared to miR KO mice.
source: The incidence of tumors was also significantly reduced in miR/p50 DKO mice, compared to miR KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: P50-deficiency significantly ameliorates the myeloproliferative disease/myeloid cancer and marrow fibrosis in aging miR-146a KO mice.
source: Together, these data show that p50-deficiency significantly ameliorates the myeloproliferative disease/myeloid cancer and marrow fibrosis in aging miR-146a KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from miR/p50 DKO mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–I.

claim: Chronic inflammation-induced or aging-associated NF-κB activation is responsible for driving HSC exhaustion, myeloproliferative disease, and myeloid cancer.
source: Overall, we have shown that chronic inflammation-induced or aging-associated NF-κB activation is responsible for driving HSC exhaustion, myeloproliferative disease, and myeloid cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from NF-κB-GFP reporter mice and miR/p50 DKO mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: After repeated LPS stimulation for 3 days, there were significantly higher percentages of BrdU+ and Ki-67+ miR-146a KO LSK cells and HSCs, compared to the WT cells, indicating an increased proliferation.
source: However, after repeated LPS stimulation for 3 days, there were significantly higher percentages of BrdU+ and Ki-67+ miR-146a KO LSK cells and HSCs, compared to the WT cells, indicating an increased proliferation (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and Ki-67 expression data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: Chronic inflammation induces increased HSC proliferation and cycling in miR-146a KO mice.
source: These data show that chronic inflammation induces increased HSC proliferation and cycling in miR-146a KO mice and underscores the particular importance of miR-146a in modulating HSC activity during chronic inflammation, as opposed to in an acute setting.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on BrdU incorporation and Ki-67 expression data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: NF-κB does not appear to directly stimulate HSPC proliferation in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: This suggests that NF-κB does not appear to directly stimulate HSPC proliferation in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that NF-κB activation and proliferation represent two largely independent populations shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Overexpression of IL-6 in bone marrow cells in mice results in myeloproliferative or lymphoproliferative disease.
source: More importantly, overexpression of IL-6 in bone marrow cells in mice results in myeloproliferative or lymphoproliferative disease (Brandt et al., 1990; Hawley et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Brandt et al., 1990; Hawley et al., 1992).

claim: IL-6 and TNFα are both upregulated in aging miR-146a KO mice.
source: IL-6 and TNFα are both upregulated in aging mR-146a KO mice (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work (Boldin et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).

claim: IL-6 expression was upregulated in both spleen and bone marrow cells of 6- to 10-month-old miR-146a KO mice, compared to WT mice.
source: Similar to what was observed in 18-month-old mice, IL-6 expression was upregulated in both spleen and bone marrow cells of miR-146a KO mice, compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: MiR/p50 DKO mice showed a level of IL-6 comparable to that of WT mice.
source: More importantly, miR/p50 DKO mice showed a level of IL-6 comparable to that of WT mice (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: IL-6, but not TNFα, showed consistently increased induction in miR-146a KO BMMs compared to WT BMMs when stimulated with LPS in vitro.
source: Furthermore, when bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs) from 8-week-old mice were stimulated with LPS in vitro, IL-6, but not TNFα, showed consistently increased induction in miR-146a KO BMMs compared to WT BMMs.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The exaggerated IL-6 induction in miR-146a KO BMMs was significantly more prominent with restimulation at a time when WT BMMs showed resistance to endotoxin restimulation.
source: Interestingly, the exaggerated IL-6 induction in miR-146a KO BMMs was significantly more prominent with restimulation at a time when WT BMMs showed resistance to endotoxin restimulation (Figure 6C; Nahid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Induction of IL-6, but not TNFα, in BMMs was highly dependent on p50.
source: In addition, induction of IL-6, but not TNFα, in BMMs was highly dependent on p50. In p50 KO BMMs, IL-6 induction was almost completely abolished (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IL-6 upregulation is an early feature in miR-146a deficiency driven HSC depletion and myeloproliferation.
source: These data suggest that IL-6 upregulation is an early feature in miR-146a deficiency driven HSC depletion and myeloproliferation and reduction in the IL-6 level may be an important factor underlying the reduced pathology when p50 is deleted.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: In the absence of IL-6, miR-146a KO mice display a partially reduced HSC defect and less myeloproliferative disease.
source: These data show that in the absence of IL-6, miR-146a KO mice display a partially reduced HSC defect and less myeloproliferative disease, indicating that upregulation of the NF-κB-responsive proinflammatory cytokine IL-6 is an important driver of the HSC defect and myeloproliferative disease in miR-146a KO mice under chronic inflammatory stress induced by aging or repeated bacterial stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from miR/IL6 DKO mice shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: Upregulation of the NF-κB-responsive proinflammatory cytokine IL-6 is an important driver of the HSC defect and myeloproliferative disease in miR-146a KO mice under chronic inflammatory stress.
source: These data show that in the absence of IL-6, miR-146a KO mice display a partially reduced HSC defect and less myeloproliferative disease, indicating that upregulation of the NF-κB-responsive proinflammatory cytokine IL-6 is an important driver of the HSC defect and myeloproliferative disease in miR-146a KO mice under chronic inflammatory stress induced by aging or repeated bacterial stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from miR/IL6 DKO mice shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: In the absence of lymphocytes, exaggerated IL-6 production is attenuated in miR-146a KO mice.
source: We found increased IL-6 production in the serum of miR-146a KO mice, compared to that of WT mice. In comparison, the serum IL-6 level in miR/Rag1 DKO mice was only modestly increased in a nonstatistically significant manner, compared to that of Rag1 KO mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Compared to miR/Rag1 DKO mice that received WT T cells, mice that received miR-146a KO T cells, but not miR/IL-6 DKO T cells, displayed bone marrow depletion of total white blood cells, myeloid progenitor cells, LSK cells, and long-term HSCs.
source: Interestingly, compared to miR/Rag1 DKO mice that received WT T cells, mice that received miR-146a KO T cells, but not miR/IL-6 DKO T cells, displayed bone marrow depletion of total white blood cells, myeloid progenitor cells, LSK cells, and long-term HSCs (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by T cell transplant data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: IL-6 overproduced by miR-146a KO T cells represents an important contributor to the HSC phenotype.
source: These data have demonstrated the particular importance of miR-146a-deficient T cells, specifically their dysregulated IL-6 production, in driving HSC and bone marrow depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on T cell transplant data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: MiR-146a KO cKit+ cells have a proliferative/survival advantage and enhanced myeloid differentiation over WT cKit+ cells under IL-6 or LPS stimulation.
source: We observed increased percentages of both cKit+ and CD11b+ KO cells in the coculture, showing that miR-146a KO cKit+ cells have a proliferative/survival advantage and enhanced myeloid differentiation over WT cKit+ cells under IL-6 or LPS stimulation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro coculture data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: KO LSK cells showed higher percentage of BrdU+ cells than WT LSK cells under IL-6 stimulation.
source: While HSCs did not have statistically significant difference in BrdU incorporation, KO LSK cells showed higher percentage of BrdU+ cells than WT LSK cells under IL-6 stimulation (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: The hematopoietic phenotypes seen in miR-146a KO mice may be mediated by IL-6 acting directly on LSK cells, but not long-term HSCs.
source: These data suggest that the hematopoietic phenotypes seen in miR-146a KO mice may be mediated by IL-6 acting directly on LSK cells, but not long-term HSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on in vitro BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7G–I.

claim: The transcript level of TRAF6 showed consistent derepression in miR-146a KO BMMs throughout LPS stimulation.
source: The transcript level of TRAF6 showed consistent derepression in miR-146a KO BMMs throughout stimulation, whereas the transcript level of IRAK1 showed perhaps an oscillating pattern but was not consistently higher than that of WT BMMs (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Derepression of TRAF6 and IRAK1 were quite modest in bulk bone marrow cells but were highest in long-term HSCs.
source: Furthermore, when HSPCs from young WT and miR-146a KO mice were analyzed for gene expression, derepression of TRAF6 and IRAK1 were quite modest in bulk bone marrow cells but were highest in long-term HSCs, suggesting that miR-146a may play a particularly important repressive role in HSCs, acting on TRAF6 and IRAK1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: MiR-146a may play a particularly important repressive role in HSCs, acting on TRAF6 and IRAK1.
source: Furthermore, when HSPCs from young WT and miR-146a KO mice were analyzed for gene expression, derepression of TRAF6 and IRAK1 were quite modest in bulk bone marrow cells but were highest in long-term HSCs, suggesting that miR-146a may play a particularly important repressive role in HSCs, acting on TRAF6 and IRAK1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The percent of GFP+ cells in nucleated peripheral blood cells transduced with pMIG-TRAF6 declined from over 40% initially to less than 10% by the end of 9 months.
source: Interestingly, the percent of GFP+ cells in nucleated peripheral blood cells transduced with either pMIG-Luc or pMIG-IRAK1 remained stable or increased slightly, whereas the GFP percentage in the pMIG-TRAF6 group declined from over 40% initially to less than 10% by the end of 9 months (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data from bone marrow transplant with TRAF6-overexpressing cells shown in Figure 8D.

claim: TRAF6-expressing mice had reduced bone marrow cellularity, compared to the control mice.
source: Histological analysis of harvested femur bones revealed that TRAF6-expressing mice had reduced bone marrow cellularity, compared to the control mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Mice receiving TRAF6-overexpressing bone marrow cells rapidly succumbed to bone marrow failure.
source: When we repeated the bone marrow transplant with 100% transduced bone marrow cells by sorting the GFP+ cells, mice receiving TRAF6-overexpressing bone marrow cells rapidly succumbed to bone marrow failure (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Upregulation of TRAF6 in HSPCs results in bone marrow failure in mice.
source: These data indicate that upregulation of TRAF6 in HSPCs results in bone marrow failure in mice, thus emphasizing the importance of tightly regulating TRAF6 level in HSPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on bone marrow transplant data with TRAF6-overexpressing cells shown in Figure 8F–I.

claim: Derepression of TRAF6 in miR-146a-deficient HSPCs could be primarily responsible for driving HSC depletion and bone marrow failure.
source: This result suggests that derepression of TRAF6 in miR-146a-deficient HSPCs could be primarily responsible for driving HSC depletion and bone marrow failure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on TRAF6 overexpression data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The cohort of unselected MDS samples showed a fourfold reduction in the level of miR-146a.
source: The cohort of unselected MDS, but not AML, samples showed a fourfold reduction in the level of miR-146a (Figure 8J), suggesting that miR-146a deficiency may be involved in MDS pathogenesis (Starczynowski et al., 2010; Rhyasen and Starczynowski, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from human bone marrow samples shown in Figure 8J.

claim: MiR-146a deficiency may be involved in MDS pathogenesis.
source: The cohort of unselected MDS, but not AML, samples showed a fourfold reduction in the level of miR-146a (Figure 8J), suggesting that miR-146a deficiency may be involved in MDS pathogenesis (Starczynowski et al., 2010; Rhyasen and Starczynowski, 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RT-qPCR data from human bone marrow samples shown in Figure 8J and cited literature (Starczynowski et al., 2010; Rhyasen and Starczynowski, 2012).

claim: The natural exposure of miR-146a KO mice to bacteria and other infectious agents may be the cause of the 'spontaneous' deterioration of HSC function, excessive myelopoiesis, and tumor formation.
source: Extrapolating from this observation, we suggest that the natural exposure of miR-146a KO mice to bacteria and other infectious agents may be the cause of the 'spontaneous' deterioration of HSC function (bone marrow failure), excessive myelopoiesis, and tumor formation that are observed in these animals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that LPS stimulation accelerates the phenotype.

claim: The excess myelopoiesis seen in normal mice as they age may be a consequence of the same process involving chronic inflammation.
source: It could well be that the excess myelopoiesis seen in normal mice as they age is a consequence of the same process (Salminen et al., 2008; Beerman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in miR-146a KO mice and cited literature (Salminen et al., 2008; Beerman et al., 2010).

claim: Infections or other perturbations activate NF-κB through TRAF6 and other signal transducers.
source: We propose the following pathway of action of miR-146a: infections or other perturbations activate NF-κB through TRAF6 and other signal transducers; the basal and NF-κB-enhanced levels of miR-146a then limit the amount of TRAF6, allowing the system to quickly return to basal NF-κB activity when the danger has passed; the transient NF-κB activation causes a transient increase in IL-6 and the IL-6 acts on the stem and progenitor cells to transiently promote proliferation and myeloid differentiation.
evidence: This is a proposed pathway based on the findings in the study.

claim: The basal and NF-κB-enhanced levels of miR-146a limit the amount of TRAF6, allowing the system to quickly return to basal NF-κB activity when the danger has passed.
source: We propose the following pathway of action of miR-146a: infections or other perturbations activate NF-κB through TRAF6 and other signal transducers; the basal and NF-κB-enhanced levels of miR-146a then limit the amount of TRAF6, allowing the system to quickly return to basal NF-κB activity when the danger has passed; the transient NF-κB activation causes a transient increase in IL-6 and the IL-6 acts on the stem and progenitor cells to transiently promote proliferation and myeloid differentiation.
evidence: This is a proposed pathway based on the findings in the study.

evidence: This is a proposed pathway based on the findings in the study.

claim: Lacking miR-146a, the action of NF-κB is extended, the production of IL-6 is exaggerated, the myelopoietic stress on the HSPCs is extended, and over time the pathological symptoms of continual myelopoiesis, bone marrow failure, and cancer emerge.
source: Lacking miR-146a, the action of NF-κB is extended, the production of IL-6 is exaggerated, the myelopoietic stress on the HSPCs is extended, and the over time the pathological symptoms of continual myelopoiesis, bone marrow failure, and cancer emerge.
evidence: This is a proposed pathway based on the findings in the study.

claim: This pathway may lead to myelodysplastic syndrome in humans.
source: This may be a pathway in humans that leads to myelodysplastic syndrome.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in mice and the observation of reduced miR-146a in human MDS samples.

claim: Chronic immune stimulation from past infection or autoimmunity increases the risk of developing myeloid malignancies, including AML, MDS, and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN).
source: First, it provides direct evidence that prolonged and uncontrolled inflammation-driven hematopoiesis can ultimately exhaust the HSC pool and lead to myeloid malignancies in genetically susceptible hosts, according nicely with some recent large scale epidemiological studies showing that chronic immune stimulation from past infection or autoimmunity increases the risk of developing myeloid malignancies, including AML, MDS, and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) (Anderson et al., 2009; Kristinsson et al., 2011; Hasselbalch, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from epidemiological studies (Anderson et al., 2009; Kristinsson et al., 2011; Hasselbalch, 2012).

claim: This study provides direct evidence that prolonged and uncontrolled inflammation-driven hematopoiesis can ultimately exhaust the HSC pool and lead to myeloid malignancies in genetically susceptible hosts.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings in the study.

claim: MiR-146a-deficient mice represent an excellent model to understand the pathogenesis of MDS.
source: Second, miR-146a-deficient mice represent an excellent model to understand the pathogenesis of MDS, a hematopoietic malignancy of older adults (median age of 70 years) (Sekeres et al., 2008) that has consistently shown reduced expression of miR-146a.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings in the study and the observation of reduced miR-146a in human MDS samples.

claim: MDS is a hematopoietic malignancy of older adults with a median age of 70 years.
source: Second, miR-146a-deficient mice represent an excellent model to understand the pathogenesis of MDS, a hematopoietic malignancy of older adults (median age of 70 years) (Sekeres et al., 2008) that has consistently shown reduced expression of miR-146a.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Sekeres et al., 2008).

claim: MDS has consistently shown reduced expression of miR-146a.
source: Second, miR-146a-deficient mice represent an excellent model to understand the pathogenesis of MDS, a hematopoietic malignancy of older adults (median age of 70 years) (Sekeres et al., 2008) that has consistently shown reduced expression of miR-146a.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from human bone marrow samples shown in Figure 8J and cited literature.

claim: Chronic inflammation may be a potential cause of the age-related decline in HSC function.
